platforms.title: Not Every Mole Is a Worry — a Changing One Is
platforms.meta_description: Most moles are harmless, but one that changes size, shape or colour needs a GP check. The NHS melanoma signs, where to look, and how to cut UV risk.
platforms.body_html:
Most adults have a scattering of moles, and almost all of them stay exactly as they are for decades. That is the point the NHS keeps coming back to on its melanoma pages: normal moles usually do not change over time. So the question worth asking is not "how many moles do I have?" but "has any of them started to look different?" A new mole, or a change in an existing one, can be the first sign of melanoma, the most serious type of skin cancer. Finding it early can mean it is easier to treat.

This article walks through what the NHS describes as the main warning signs, the less obvious places melanoma can appear, and the habits that make a change easier to catch. It is general health information and does not replace a conversation with a GP.

What makes a melanoma look different from an ordinary mole

Melanoma starts in the cells that make skin pigment. Because those cells are scattered all over the body, a melanoma can turn up anywhere, though the NHS notes it is more common in areas often exposed to the sun, although it can appear on skin that rarely sees daylight. It usually shows up as a mole-like mark rather than a lump, which is why it is easy to dismiss.

The NHS compares a typical mole with a melanoma on a few points. Normal moles are usually round with smooth edges, whereas melanomas are often an uneven shape, with two different shaped halves and uneven edges. Normal moles tend to be a single colour; melanomas are often a mix of two or more colours. Ordinary moles are usually small, about the size of the end of a pencil or smaller, while melanomas tend to be bigger, often more than 6mm wide. The NHS adds a caveat: they can sometimes be smaller if they are diagnosed early, so size alone does not rule anything out.

The single most useful sign is change. According to the NHS, a mole that changes size, shape or colour may be a melanoma. Other things to look out for are moles that become swollen and sore, bleed, itch or turn crusty.

Some rarer types start in places people rarely look. The NHS lists the soles of the feet, the palms of the hands, the eyes and the genitals. It also notes that people with black or brown skin have a lower chance of getting melanoma, but when they do, it is most often on the soles, the palms or under a nail. That is why the GP advice includes a dark area under a nail that has not been caused by an injury, and any new or unusual mark on the palms or soles that has not gone away after a few weeks.

As for causes, the NHS states that ultraviolet light, from the sun and from sunbeds, is the most common cause of melanoma. You are more likely to get it if you have pale skin that burns easily, red or blonde hair, blue or green eyes, a large number of freckles or moles, a history of sunburn or heavy sunbed use, or a personal or family history of skin cancer.

3 habits that make a changing mole easier to spot

Look at your whole skin, including the hidden parts. The NHS suggests checking your skin for any unusual changes and using a mirror, or asking a partner or friend, for areas you cannot see. Include the soles of your feet, your palms and your nails, because those are the places rarer melanomas begin and the places nobody glances at.

Keep a record so "change" means something. Memory is a poor ruler. A dated photo of any mole you are unsure about, taken at the same distance with a coin or ruler beside it, lets you compare size, shape and colour a few weeks later. That matters because change is the warning sign the NHS stresses most, and a GP will want to know what has changed and when.

Cut UV exposure where it is easy to do. The NHS advice for lowering melanoma risk is practical: stay out of the sun during the hottest part of the day, which in the UK is 11am to 3pm; cover arms and legs and wear a wide-brimmed hat and UV-protective sunglasses; use sunscreen with at least SPF 30 and at least 4-star UVA protection, reapplied regularly; and protect babies and children, whose skin is much more sensitive. Avoiding sunbeds removes an artificial UV source entirely.

Going back over the four checks

To recap the signs the NHS describes: an uneven shape or edges, a mix of colours, a mole that is larger than usual, and above all a mole that is changing. Add the extra flags of soreness, bleeding, itching or crusting, and the hidden sites on soles, palms and nails.

If any of these fits, see a GP. The NHS says to book an appointment if a mole has changed size, shape or colour, is painful or itchy, or is inflamed, bleeding or crusty. At the appointment, tell the GP what has changed and whether you or anyone in your family has had skin cancer. The GP may photograph the mole and send it to a dermatologist to review, which is called teledermatology, or refer you urgently to a specialist if they think it could be cancer. An urgent referral does not mean you definitely have cancer; it means the mole is being looked at properly and quickly.

Sources: NHS, "Symptoms of melanoma skin cancer" and "Causes of melanoma skin cancer" (page last reviewed 15 July 2026).
